doc.title: Bill Kirchner interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2021

title: Parents' attitude and the 1965 Pittsburgh jazz festival
summary: His parents paid for lessons but did not want a musician's career; at a George Wein festival in Pittsburgh he heard Hines, Getz, Coltrane and Ellington with Strayhorn, which set his path. He then followed late-night jazz radio.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Can I guess that your parents looked askance at a music career?

Good guess. Oh yeah. I mean no they didn’t want me to have a career as a musician, although I mean they did encourage my interest in music. I mean they paid for music lessons for me for years, and I should tell this story, going back to the Ellington. In 1965 I was just short of my twelfth birthday and I had this neophyte’s interest in jazz. So there was a three day jazz festival in Pittsburgh at the civic arena that George Wein was producing. And Pittsburgh is about an hour or so’s drive from Youngstown. So for my upcoming twelfth birthday my parents gave me an early birthday present and said we’ll take you to this festival on a Saturday night. So we went to Pittsburgh to the civic arena, and the bill for the one night, it was a Saturday night, the opening act was this local guy, a piano player named Walt Harper with his group; and then Earl Hines with a trio; Carmen McRae with Norman Simmons’ trio; Stan Getz’s quartet with Gary Burton, Steve Swallow and Roy Haynes; John Coltrane’s quartet with McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison and Elvin Jones; and the Ellington band with Billy Strayhorn as a guest because

Strayhorn was from Pittsburgh, as was Earl Hines. So this was kind of a homecoming for both of them. So this was the bill for one night. And I mean that was the night that basically set me on my career path, even though my parents didn’t realize it at the time nor would they have approved if they’d known it, but I mean that really set me on my career path I mean as far as solidifying a serious interest in jazz. Up to that point I’d been doing my best to listen to top 40 radio to conform to the interest of my schoolmates. But after that top 40 radio just went down the toilet. I couldn’t care less after that. I started using whatever allowance money I had to buy LPs. My parents bought a stereo that I could play the LPs on, and other than that, you know there were some syndicated jazz radio shows like Sid Mark in Philadelphia had a syndicated jazz radio show that I would listen to on Saturday nights. And there was a 50,000 watt clear channel station in Rochester, New York, WHAM, that had a five hour jazz show from midnight to five in the morning that I would listen to on my transistor radio, especially when I was on holidays from school. I would just lie in bed with my transistor. This is late 60s, early 70s. And there were two different DJs. The first guy was a guy named Bill Ardis, and then his successor was a guy named Harry Abraham. And they played really hip stuff, you know whatever the new LP releases were. I mean I heard, I remember one night I was listening to the radio and this kind of funk type thing came on and I was wondering what is this? Is this Cannonball Adderley or something? And it turned out to be Miles Davis from “Miles in the Sky” doing that tune called “Stuff” which was the first time Herbie Hancock recorded on a Fender Rhodes. So I heard that on Harry Abraham’s show. So I heard, I guess at that point I had found outlets that were — even in Youngstown, Ohio I could hear what was going on.
